name: Bay Area Birds: Sight and Sound
description: See it and hear it: the everyday birds of Bay Area yards, parks, chaparral, and shoreline. Photo ID cards plus song and call mnemonics, with field marks and lookalike tips in the details.

fields.extra: Aphelocoma californica. Crestless azure-blue jay with a gray-brown back, whitish throat, and partial blue necklace. Loud, bold, and everywhere in Berkeley; buries acorns all fall. Steller's jay is the darker, crested one up in the conifers.
Calypte anna. Male's whole crown and throat flash iridescent rose-pink. The Bay Area's year-round hummingbird, singing a scratchy, buzzy song from exposed perches even in December.

fields.front: The loud single "chirp!" at the bottom of an Anna's hummingbird's courtship dive is made with what?
fields.extra: The male climbs high, plummets past the female, and the airflow through spread tail feathers produces the sound — shown by UC Berkeley researchers. Not a vocal sound at all.

Haemorhous mexicanus. Streaky brown finch; males wear raspberry-red on the head and chest. The default small bird at Bay Area feeders, with a long cheerful warble that trails off in a slurred "wheer".

Melozone crissalis. The default plain matte-brown bird of Berkeley yards, with a rusty patch under the tail. Scratches on the ground, usually in faithful pairs, giving sharp metallic "chink" notes. Its flashy cousin is the spotted towhee.

Sayornis nigricans. Dapper sooty-black flycatcher with a crisp white belly; pumps its tail while perched, then sallies out for insects and returns to the same perch. Loves patios, fountains, and creek edges.
Zenaida macroura. Slim, soft gray-brown dove with a long pointed white-edged tail and black wing spots. Its wings whistle sharply when it bursts into flight.

fields.front: The soft, owl-like daytime cooing ("coo-OO-oo, oo, oo") from a Bay Area wire or rooftop is which bird?
fields.extra: The classic beginner trap: it sounds like an owl but owls rarely call in daylight. The mournful coo is the male's song and the source of the bird's name.

Corvus brachyrhynchos. All-black, with a fan-shaped tail and the familiar "caw". Berkeley's crows stream overhead in big evening flights to communal roosts. The heavier, croaking version is the common raven.
Corvus corax. Crow's giant cousin: massive bill, shaggy throat feathers, and long wings built for soaring. Increasingly common right in Bay Area cities, not just wild coast.

fields.front: A deep, hollow croaking "gronk-gronk" overhead means which corvid?
fields.extra: Crows caw, ravens croak. If the voice sounds like it needs a throat lozenge, it's a raven.

fields.front: In flight overhead, what tail shape separates a raven from a crow?
fields.back: A raven's tail is wedge-shaped (diamond); a crow's is a rounded fan.
fields.extra: Backup checks: ravens soar and glide on longer wings; crows flap steadily. Ravens travel in pairs, crows in mobs.
Turdus migratorius. Brick-red breast, gray back, upright hop-and-stop posture on lawns. Its rich caroling "cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio" is often the first song of a Bay Area dawn.

fields.front: Small sparrow hopping under Bay Area feeders: crisp black hood, warm brown back, pink bill, white outer tail feathers flashing as it flits away. What is it?
fields.extra: Junco hyemalis. Our West Coast birds wear the black executioner's hood over a brown body; eastern birds are plain slate-gray. Song is a simple loose one-pitch trill. Abundant in Berkeley year-round.

Poecile rufescens. Tiny acrobat with a dark cap and bib and a rich chestnut back — the only chickadee you'll normally see in the Bay Area. Constantly moving through oaks and conifers, often with bushtit flocks.

fields.front: Which Bay Area bird gives a fast, hoarse, wheezy "chick-a-dee-dee" but never a clear whistled song?
fields.extra: Unlike the black-capped chickadee of the East and far North, the chestnut-backed has no whistled "fee-bee" song — its scratchy chatter is all you get.

Sturnus vulgaris. Chunky, short-tailed blackbird-shaped bird: iridescent purple-green with a yellow bill in breeding plumage, white-spangled in winter. Introduced; wheezes, clicks, and mimics other birds and car alarms.
Mimus polyglottos. Slim gray bird with big white wing flashes that show in flight and in its wing-lifting display. Holds a territory year-round and defends it loudly.

fields.front: A bird running through an endless medley — each phrase repeated about three times — at 2 a.m. under a Berkeley streetlight is which species?
fields.extra: The triple repeat is the tell: mockingbirds cycle each borrowed phrase a few times before switching. Unmated males famously sing all night in spring.
Callipepla californica. Plump gray-brown quail with a comma-shaped head plume and scaled belly — California's state bird. Runs in coveys through brush in Tilden and other parks.

fields.front: Which Bay Area bird shouts a loud three-syllable "Chi-ca-GO!" from the brush?
fields.extra: The male's assembly call, with the accent on the last syllable. Handy for a Chicago transplant: the bird that calls your old hometown is the state bird of your new one.

Meleagris gallopavo. Introduced to California and now brazenly at home on Berkeley streets and the Cal campus, roosting in tall trees at night. Gobbling toms and trains of poults are a local institution.

Cyanocitta stelleri. Deep blue with a sooty-black head and tall shaggy crest — the only crested jay in the West. In the Bay Area it's the jay of the conifers: Berkeley Hills, Tilden, Muir Woods. Harsh "shack-shack-shack" calls.

fields.front: You hear a perfect red-tailed hawk scream coming from inside a tree canopy. What should you suspect?
fields.extra: Both Steller's jays and scrub-jays do convincing red-tail impressions, possibly to scatter competitors from food. A real red-tail screams from the open sky, not from dense foliage.

Pipilo maculatus. Black hood, rufous flanks, white-spotted wings, red eye. Makes a racket two-foot-scratching in leaf litter; call is a rising catlike "mreee". Towhee siblings: this is the flashy one, the California towhee is the plain brown one.

Baeolophus inornatus. Small, plain gray, with a short pointed crest — the personality of a chickadee in an unmarked uniform. True to its name, it sticks to oak woodland and sings a whistled "peter-peter-peter".
Psaltriparus minimus. Tiny gray puffball with a long tail, almost never alone: flocks of 10-40 tumble through hedges trading soft "spit" contact notes, then move on. Weaves a hanging sock of a nest.
Thryomanes bewickii. Brown wren with a bold white eyebrow and a long tail it cocks and flicks sideways. Sings a loud, varied, buzzy-then-sweet song from Bay Area brush piles and gardens.
Chamaea fasciata. Plain gray-brown skulker with a pale eye and a long, usually-cocked tail; barely flies and almost never leaves dense chaparral. You'll hear a hundred for every one you see.

fields.front: Which chaparral bird's song is a series of pips accelerating into a trill, like a ping-pong ball settling on a table?
fields.extra: The "bouncing ball" is the signature sound of California chaparral — Tilden's scrub hillsides ring with it. Learn it and you've identified a bird you may never actually see.

Melospiza melodia. Streaky brown sparrow whose breast streaks converge in a central dark spot. Common in Bay Area creek brush and marsh edges; pumps its tail in flight. Sparrow siblings: crowned sparrows have bold head stripes instead of breast streaks.

fields.front: Which sparrow's song starts with two or three clear notes then tumbles into a jumble — remembered as "maids-maids-maids, put-on-your-tea-kettle-ettle-ettle"?
fields.extra: The clear opening notes are the tell; every male sings his own variations on the theme, all year, from an exposed perch.

Zonotrichia leucophrys. Clean gray sparrow with a boldly black-and-white striped crown and a pink-orange bill. Winter flocks blanket Bay Area parks; some coastal birds stay all year. Sibling: golden-crowned has a yellow forehead patch, not stripes.

Zonotrichia atricapilla. Dusky winter sparrow with a dull yellow central crown patch bordered in black. Arrives from Alaska each fall, scratches under Bay Area feeders all winter, gone by May. Sibling: white-crowned wears crisp zebra stripes instead.

fields.front: Which winter sparrow sings three clear descending whistles, remembered as "oh, dear, me"?
fields.extra: The minor-key lament drifts from Bay Area hedges all winter. Gold Rush miners heard it as "no gold here".

Spinus psaltria. Tiny yellow-bellied finch; males have a black cap and greenish back. The Bay Area's everyday goldfinch, giving plaintive wheezy calls and jangly song from treetops. The bigger, brighter American goldfinch is scarcer here.
Sialia mexicana. Deep blue head and wings over a rusty-orange chest. Perches on fences and low branches in open Bay Area parkland, dropping to the grass for insects; often checks out nest boxes.

Bombycilla cedrorum. Sleek crested bird with a black mask and a yellow-tipped tail, looking airbrushed. Winter flocks descend on Bay Area berry trees, strip them, and vanish; listen for high thin "sreee" calls overhead.

Melanerpes formicivorus. Clown-faced woodpecker: white eye, red cap, harlequin black-and-white pattern. Lives in noisy family groups that drill thousands of acorn holes into 'granary' trees and poles all over East Bay oak country.

fields.front: Which woodpecker laughs a raucous "waka-waka-waka" from Bay Area oaks?
fields.extra: The call sounds like cartoon laughter and gives away the whole colony at once.

Colaptes auratus. Big brown woodpecker with a black chest crescent and spotted belly; our western 'red-shafted' birds flash salmon-red under the wings and tail, and the white rump shows in flight. Feeds on the ground, eating ants.

Dryobates pubescens. Sparrow-sized black-and-white woodpecker with a white back stripe and stubby bill; males add a red nape spot. Bay Area lookalike: Nuttall's woodpecker has a barred (striped) back with no white patch.

Agelaius phoeniceus. Males are jet black with red-and-yellow shoulder patches, flared while singing a gurgling "conk-la-reee!" from cattails. Fills every Bay Area marsh, including the Berkeley waterfront.

Euphagus cyanocephalus. The parking-lot blackbird: males glossy black with a purple-green sheen and a staring yellow eye, females plain brown with a dark eye. Struts around Bay Area cafes and lots begging crumbs.

Charadrius vociferus. Slender plover with two black chest bands, at home on ballfields and gravel lots far from water. Screams its own name — "kill-deer!" — and lures intruders from its nest with a fake broken-wing act.

Ardea herodias. Four feet of gray-blue patience, standing statue-still in Bay Area shallows and even hunting gophers in park meadows. Flies with slow wingbeats and its neck folded in an S, croaking hoarsely when flushed.

fields.front: A tall, pure-white heron on the bay shore with a yellow bill and all-black legs and feet is which species?
fields.extra: Ardea alba. Egret siblings: great egret = yellow bill, black feet; snowy egret = black bill, yellow feet. Size helps too — the great is nearly heron-sized.

fields.front: A small white heron with a black bill, black legs, and bright yellow feet — 'golden slippers' — is which species?
fields.extra: Egretta thula. The yellow feet are the clincher, often used to stir up prey in the shallows. Mirror-image sibling: the great egret has a yellow bill and black feet.

fields.front: Huge gray-brown seabirds gliding in single file just above the water, then plunge-diving headfirst — which species?
fields.extra: Pelecanus occidentalis. A conservation comeback story (DDT nearly wiped them out). The bay's other pelican, the American white, is bigger, swims and scoops instead, and never dives.

fields.front: The blackish waterbird perched on Bay pilings with its wings spread wide to dry is which species?
fields.extra: Nannopterum auritum. Its feathers soak through (less oil means less buoyancy for chasing fish underwater), so it must hang itself out to dry. Swims low with an up-tilted hooked bill; big colonies nest on the Bay Bridge.

fields.front: The default large gull of the bay and coast — dark slate back, pink legs, heavy yellow bill with a red spot — is which species?
fields.extra: Larus occidentalis. The year-round resident breeder; winter brings a confusing crowd of visiting gull species, but the dark-backed, pink-legged local is this one. Chicks peck the red bill spot to beg food.

fields.front: A white-bellied raptor with a dark eye-stripe hovers over the bay, then plunges feet-first for a fish. What is it?
fields.extra: Pandion haliaetus. Flies on crooked M-shaped wings; nests on cranes, pilings, and light towers along the Richmond and Oakland waterfront. Feet-first plunge = osprey; head-first = brown pelican.

Cathartes aura. The Bay Area's constant overhead glider: holds its two-toned wings in a shallow V and teeters side to side, rarely flapping. Tiny naked red head. Steady flat wings and powerful flaps mean hawk or eagle instead.
Buteo jamaicensis. Bulky soaring hawk with a brick-red tail (adults) and a streaky belly band; the raptor on freeway light poles and fence posts everywhere in the Bay Area.

fields.front: The long, raspy, descending scream — "keeeeer!" — used in movies for every eagle belongs to which bird?
fields.extra: Hollywood dubs it over bald eagles, whose real voice is a weak chirping. If you hear it from inside a tree canopy, suspect a mimicking jay.

Astur cooperii. The backyard bird-hunter: long banded tail, short rounded wings, flap-flap-glide flight. If a hawk ambushes your feeder or dashes through Berkeley trees after songbirds, it's this accipiter, not a red-tail.

fields.front: Which raptor famously nests on UC Berkeley's Campanile?
fields.extra: The 'Cal Falcons' nest cam is a Berkeley obsession. Peregrines are the fastest animals on Earth, stooping on pigeons at over 200 mph; they also nest on Bay Area bridges and towers.

fields.front: Deep, muffled hoots at dusk in a stuttered rhythm — "Who's awake? Me too" — belong to which owl?
fields.extra: Bubo virginianus. Pairs duet from Bay Area eucalyptus and pine groves, the female's hoots higher-pitched. Owl siblings: the barn owl never hoots — it screeches.

fields.front: A long, harsh, hissing screech overhead on a Bay Area night — no hooting at all — is which owl?
fields.extra: Tyto alba. A ghostly white-faced owl that hunts over parks and fields and nests in palms and building cavities all over Berkeley. Owl siblings: hoots mean great horned, screeches mean barn owl.
